abstract: MIT FutureTech researchers (arXiv 2607.08920, July 2026) measure AI adoption among S&P 500 firms from 2016 to 2025 using a rubric applied to SEC 10-K filings, where false or misleading statements carry legal liability, to separate deep adoption from AI hype. In 2025, 11% of S&P 500 firms had AI deeply integrated into business processes and a further 10% used AI in producing goods or delivering services: 21% in total, more than four times the 5% of 2022. Adoption among non-tech firms is accelerating slowly. The technology sector adopts aggressively and accounts for two-thirds of deep integration. Profitability traces a J-curve from no adoption to deep adoption, but adopters show no differences in capex or productivity.
keyFindings: 21% of S&P 500 firms had deep (11%) or production-level (10%) AI adoption in 2025, according to 10-K filings.
Adoption more than quadrupled from 5% in 2022.
The technology sector accounts for two-thirds of deeply integrated enterprise adoption.
Firm profitability shows a J-curve as firms move to deep adoption, but there are no differences in capex or productivity.
Among technology firms only, adoption is higher for firms with more employees and higher Tobin's q.
methodology: Firm-year panel of S&P 500 constituents from 2016 to 2025. A novel rubric scores 10-K filing text for the depth of AI adoption (deep integration in business processes; use in production or service delivery; lower tiers). Adoption is then regressed on financial outcomes (profitability, capex, productivity, Tobin's q, employment). Funded by the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation.
qualifiers: Tier 2: unrefereed arXiv working paper. It covers only the S&P 500, the largest US public firms, so it cannot stand in for economy-wide adoption; the authors frame these firms as bellwethers. 10-K disclosure captures what firms choose to report as material, so it likely undercounts informal or employee-level GenAI use, which is a deliberately higher bar than Census BTOS. Associations with financial outcomes are not causal.
